Shelly's Legacy

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A Cape Town woman has been transforming lives for decades by providing wheelchair related services to families across South Africa.

Unique Selling Point:
Shona McDonald has been changing lives since her own daughter, Shelly, was born with severe disabilities more than forty years ago. Her daughter was born with cerebral palsy because of medical negligence. At the time, doctors advised Shona to put her child in a home. She refused. She also did not take legal action against the hospital as she wanted to turn it into something positive. Instead, she approached the biomedical engineering department at UCT and asked them to help her build the first paediatric electric wheelchair in Africa.


Summary:
She embarked on finding therapists and accessing information from abroad (it was before the internet) to try and understand what was possible and what was being done overseas.

She researched how she could assist her daughter to sit up straight so she could see her mother, and she looked into ways her daughter could communicate more effectively. With the help of UCT, her child’s wheelchair for outdoors with full body support, that could go up and down, and in which she could move around herself, was built. Shelly was able to drive herself around by the age of eighteen months.

Shona started an organization called Interface, that focused on helping non-verbal people communicate. She built different types of chairs for different children from her garage and did fundraising for those who couldn’t afford it. She realized the need was much greater than she had imagined.

By 1992, she had outgrown her garage and realized she needed to turn it into a business. That was when she launched "Shonaquip Social Enterprise" which provides wheelchair related services to families across South Africa. Now, she has 85 people in her team and they work across seven countries. They make equipment for people living in rural areas, where wheelchairs are used off road. Furthermore, Shona's wheelchairs are designed to help children improve their function.

Assistive devices are just a tool, but Shona’s work also looks at early child development, play for all, assistive technology and a parent network. She launched a parent network during Covid. She wanted to give parents knowledge and trains parents online three times a month. Nine hundred parents are trained every two weeks. They are upskilled and can run advocacy and anti bias workshops in their communities. Results of the training provide Shona with data that she reports to government to show where systems are failing.

Shona has a fully inclusive team, with disabled people working in the factory as well. Her factory is in Ottery. She lives in Noordhoek with her three daughters. They all live on one property.







Further information:
One man on the assembly team is an ex paralympic ping pong player. He had polio as a child so is paralysed from the waist down. Her whole focus is around how to ensure society values disabled people equally. There is also a lot of focus on making sure government has the right policies in place. When she started there was no such thing as a paediatric wheelchair tender. Now there is. Most children attending government hospitals, are now able to get one within a year. But, there are budget constraints. Shona has a wheelchair fund that helps kids who fall through the cracks.

We will also speak to Vic McKinney who works with Shona. He was rendered quadriplegic after a devastating car accident in 1987. His father died in the accident. He became friends with Shona when she helped him design his first wheelchair. Together they confront stigma and are trying to change the lives of people with disabilities and bring an end to prejudice.

Script:


VO 1 Vic McKinney has always loved creating art.

VO 2 He has a unique talent. Each artwork the result of countless hours of focus and dedication.

VO 3 But, he didn’t always paint in this way.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 595 / Day 2 / Cam 1) 12:41 I had just turned nineteen after a great weekend and my life changed in an instant.

FADE TO BLACK

VO 4 Vic was studying fine art at the University of Cape Town. A car accident left him paralysed from the neck down. His father, who was driving, was killed.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 595 / Day 2 / Cam 1) 13:10 I was in good spirits, ready to take on the world, and then suddenly I couldn’t move and I’d lost my dad who was my hero.

VO 5 It was hard to adjust to life as a quadriplegic.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (clip 594/ Day 2) 26:59 I had this whole thing of nothing will ever be good enough again. And that’s nonsense. You don’t know until you try.

VO 6 It’s a positive outlook that initially proved elusive.

UPSOUND Vic (Clip 594 /Day 2) 15:33 I was very much a lost soul I’d say for the first ten years after the accident. UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 594 / Day / Cam 1) 14:03 For a while I rejected my life, in fact for a long while. I didn’t want to live long. I didn’t want to reach thirty. I could not see a future for myself.

VO 7 Working with disabled children in townships, his perspective began to shift.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 594 / Day 2) 15:00 I grew up like a little spoilt white kid in Apartheid, it was a complete change, and I saw the other half of the country that I didn’t know about much.Time code 15:15 Art was important to me, children were important to me. So I started to get involved with day centres for kids with disabilities.

VO 8 And then, more than thirty years ago, he crossed paths with a woman who would have an extraordinary impact on his life. They shared the same mission - to work towards more inclusion for people with disabilities. Her name was Shona McDonald.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney / SSE Board Member (Clip 594 / Day 2) 09:32 We just got talking. She said come for lunch. And I’ve never been the same since. 09:37 We were like minded.

VO 9 Shona’s life too had taken an unexpected turn when her second daughter Shelly was born in 1982.

UPSOUND Shona McDonald (clip 533 / Day 1 / Cam 1) 01:51 I had a caesar with Shelly and during the ceasar something went wrong. They didn’t tell me what but I lost a great deal of blood. 04:00 The advice from the medical profession was to put Shelly in a home and have another child.

VO 10 Shelly was diagnosed with cerebral palsy … the result of a birth injury.

UPSOUND Shona McDonald / Shonaquip Social Enterprise (Clip 533 / Day 1 / Cam 1) 03:06 Everybody came round to the house and everybody was crying and upset, and talking about suing doctors. But, for me, it was about well what can I do to make it better. To fix it. To help. So that she can really live her best life.

Claire 04:50 (C0006.MP4) Card 1 / Day 1 At that time it wasn’t like there was the internet, you couldn’t google things, so how are you finding out ways to best care for your child?

UPSOUND Shona McDonald / Shonaquip Social Enterprise (Day 1/ Clip 533) 04:52 I was very lucky in that one of my cousins lived in England, and she started sending me by mail lots of resources and books of what was happening overseas. I found a photograph of an electric wheelchair for a small child, and I started playing around at building her one.

VO 11 She asked for help from an engineer from the University of Cape Town and by the time Shelly was 18 months old, she was mobile. (photos of Shelly in electric wheelchair sent on wetransfer)

UPSOUND Shona (Clip 534 / Day 1) 02:43 As far as we know, it was the very first electric wheelchair built in Africa, certainly no chair has been built for a child as young as 18 months old.

NATSOUND (Day 1 / Cam 2 / Card 1 / Clip 0011.MP4) 02:54 Formal lessons. 03:01 And then once she’d learnt to read we managed to get her into the mainstream school.

VO 12 Shona was determined to make Shelly as comfortable and happy as possible - to help her communicate and interact with other children.

NATSOUND(Day 1 Card 2 / Cam 2 / Clip C0001.MP4) 00:04 This is her two sisters and her two best friends.

UPSOUND Shona McDonald 08:07 Even my parents were dropping little notes in my postbox with homes that I could explore. 08:16 For me the big revelation was people are fearful of what’s different and how can I change that.

VO 13 She refused to hide Shelly away, and instead started a not for profit organisation for people unable to speak. Shona met many parents of children affected by a range of disabilities. They asked her for help.

VO 14 From her garage, Shona began producing wheelchairs for their children too.

VO 15 Now, Shonaquip Social Enterprise employs over 80 people, its factory designing and manufacturing thousands of wheelchairs for private clients and government tenders.

UPSOUND Shona McDonald (Clip 533/Day2/Cam 1) 26:39 As we were approached by more and more parents, that automatically shifted to where we started working with government therapists, so now Namibia has a great wheelchair tender, Botswana on board, and we’re working with a number of other countries.

VO 16 Vic is on the board of Shonaquip Social Enterprise and even has a wheelchair named after him.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (clip 594 / Day 2) 09:58 Shona’s helped me develop my chair and develop a better quality of chair. 10:34 I need trunk support around my ribs and waist so it became the Vic chair.

VO 17 About fifteen percent of Shona’s employees are disabled - including James Houston.

UPSOUND James Houston (Cam 1/ Day 1 / Clip 423) 00:43 I have polio at the age of three years old. 17:34 I was walking normal then I just went outside the gate and I just collapsed.

VO 18 Polio is an infectious viral disease that affects the nervous system and can cause paralysis. For much of his youth, James was able to use crutches to get around. These days, after several shoulder operations, he mostly relies on his wheelchair. And he recognises just how important it is for his quality of life.

UPSOUND James Houston / Shonaquip Social Enterprise Cam 1 / Clip 423 Time code 5:06 In 2006, then I came to Shona’s house, she was working from the garage She ask me can you do upholstery, I said yes I can. 05:54 The challenge was big. And I take it on. And I never stop since then. (there’s a photo of James sitting in wooden chair in Shona’s garage)

CLAIRE Clip 0002.MP4 Day 1 / Card 1 / Cam 2 06:46 It’s more than a job.

UPSOUND James Houston / Shonaquip Social Enterprise (Clip 423 / Day 1/ Cam 1) 06:35 It’s more than a job. You can say that again. You have to make them smile. Some of them they can’t talk but they can smiled to you and say thumbs up for what you are doing for me.

VO 19 James is a talented athlete and played basketball in the paralympics. Now, he coaches others. (photos of his medals)

UPSOUND James Houston (Clip 423 / Day 1) 28:51 I have three of them, Paralympian athletes, who came out of my hands. And I said to youngsters, if you need my help, you can arrange with your parents to fetch me, we can go to the field and I can train you soccer, javelin, whatever you want.

VO 20 James has travelled abroad for sports events, and seen what’s possible when transport systems are designed with disabled people in mind.

UPSOUND James Houston (Clip 434 / Day 1) 02:22 Its unbelievable what I’ve seen in Japan. It’s unbelievable what I see in Australia. 02:33 Everything was perfect for wheelchairs, even for people with crutches. 03:03 In South Africa, there’s nothing like that.

UPSOUND Shona McDonald (Clip 533 / Day 1) 28:54 Many of our staff, they have to ride to work in their wheelchairs, sometimes kilometers. In winter, it’s grim.

VO 21 Transport gives children an opportunity for inclusive education - something Shelly was lucky to have.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 595 / Day 2 / Cam 1) 05:35 We have about 30 to 35 000 wheelchair users in Cape Town, but we don’t see them. Because they can’t access trains or whatever or get on public transport. (CLIP 594) 07:42 I was very privileged to have my own accessible vehicle. Gives a heightened sense of responsibility. Motivates me to try and change things and policies. And fight for rights.

VO 22 And having the right wheelchair is crucial.

UPSOUND Shona 18:32 Having a wheelchair for a child is a body prosthetic, it’s holding them, holding their bodies safely in a position to grow that doesn't cause secondary health problems.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 595 / Day 2) 06:58 I wouldn’t be able to do my art and push my own boundaries if I didn’t have the correct device. (Clip 594 / Day 2) 28:14 I think I’m an example of what’s possible when you have the right support, many people look at the wheelchair and think you can’t be in a relationship or contribute in some way.

VO 23 Vic met his wife Emma in 2007. They married several years later and they now have two sons - Benjamin and Jamie. He’s also a lecturer and is doing his post doctorate in the division of Disability and Rehabilitation Studies at Stellenbosch University.

CLAIRE: 00:56 What is life like for you and your two boys?
UPSOUND Emma McKinney 01:01. It’s pretty normal it’s average, we have to have certain accommodations, I’m his wife, I’m not his medical carer, we’ve got those and we’re very privileged to have carers in our lives.

VO 24 Vic could never have imagined that such a profoundly devastating accident, would set him on a path to making a difference to so many others.

UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 594/ Day 2 / Cam 1) 23:54 It’s amazing to be here now. I need to remind myself, and I do often, just to be grateful for what I have. 25:47 What’s also been really amazing has been to see my disability through the eyes of my children, it’s so refreshing. When they kids, doing kids drawings, there’s dad in a wheelchair, i’m not separate. (sent photo of kids drawing on wetransfer)

VO 25 For Shona too, producing wheelchairs for thousands of children, was not what she had planned. . Having a daughter with cerebral palsy kickstarted a whole new way of life. .

UPSOUND Shona McDonald (Day 1 / Clip 534) 09:30 I think we all plan too much about what life’s going to look like, instead of just embracing what happens. (Clip 534) 07:50 Life’s taken me on a journey I hadn’t expected, but one I really enjoy, I wake up every day, ready for another challenge.

UPSOUND James Houston / Shonaquip Social Enterprise Cam 1 / Clip 423 Time code 5:06 In 2006, then I came to Shona’s house, she was working from the garage She ask me can you do upholstery, I said yes I can. 05:54 The challenge was big. And I take it on. And I never stop since then. (there’s a photo of James sitting in wooden chair in Shona’s garage) CLAIRE Clip 0002.MP4 Day 1 / Card 1 / Cam 2 06:46 It’s more than a job. UPSOUND James Houston / Shonaquip Social Enterprise (Clip 423 / Day 1/ Cam 1) 06:35 It’s more than a job. You can say that again. You have to make them smile. Some of them they can’t talk but they can smiled to you and say thumbs up for what you are doing for me. VO 19 James is a talented athlete and played basketball in the paralympics. Now, he coaches others. (photos of his medals) UPSOUND James Houston (Clip 423 / Day 1) 28:51 I have three of them, Paralympian athletes, who came out of my hands. And I said to youngsters, if you need my help, you can arrange with your parents to fetch me, we can go to the field and I can train you soccer, javelin, whatever you want. VO 20 James has travelled abroad for sports events, and seen what’s possible when transport systems are designed with disabled people in mind. UPSOUND James Houston (Clip 434 / Day 1) 02:22 Its unbelievable what I’ve seen in Japan. It’s unbelievable what I see in Australia. 02:33 Everything was perfect for wheelchairs, even for people with crutches. 03:03 In South Africa, there’s nothing like that. UPSOUND Shona McDonald (Clip 533 / Day 1) 28:54 Many of our staff, they have to ride to work in their wheelchairs, sometimes kilometers. In winter, it’s grim. VO 21 Transport gives children an opportunity for inclusive education - something Shelly was lucky to have. UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 595 / Day 2 / Cam 1) 05:35 We have about 30 to 35 000 wheelchair users in Cape Town, but we don’t see them. Because they can’t access trains or whatever or get on public transport. (CLIP 594) 07:42 I was very privileged to have my own accessible vehicle. Gives a heightened sense of responsibility. Motivates me to try and change things and policies. And fight for rights. VO 22 And having the right wheelchair is crucial. UPSOUND Shona 18:32 Having a wheelchair for a child is a body prosthetic, it’s holding them, holding their bodies safely in a position to grow that doesn't cause secondary health problems. UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 595 / Day 2) 06:58 I wouldn’t be able to do my art and push my own boundaries if I didn’t have the correct device. (Clip 594 / Day 2) 28:14 I think I’m an example of what’s possible when you have the right support, many people look at the wheelchair and think you can’t be in a relationship or contribute in some way. VO 23 Vic met his wife Emma in 2007. They married several years later and they now have two sons - Benjamin and Jamie. He’s also a lecturer and is doing his post doctorate in the division of Disability and Rehabilitation Studies at Stellenbosch University. CLAIRE: 00:56 What is life like for you and your two boys? UPSOUND Emma McKinney 01:01. It’s pretty normal it’s average, we have to have certain accommodations, I’m his wife, I’m not his medical carer, we’ve got those and we’re very privileged to have carers in our lives. VO 24 Vic could never have imagined that such a profoundly devastating accident, would set him on a path to making a difference to so many others. UPSOUND Vic McKinney (Clip 594/ Day 2 / Cam 1) 23:54 It’s amazing to be here now. I need to remind myself, and I do often, just to be grateful for what I have. 25:47 What’s also been really amazing has been to see my disability through the eyes of my children, it’s so refreshing. When they kids, doing kids drawings, there’s dad in a wheelchair, i’m not separate. (sent photo of kids drawing on wetransfer) VO 25 For Shona too, producing wheelchairs for thousands of children, was not what she had planned. . Having a daughter with cerebral palsy kickstarted a whole new way of life. . metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A Cape Town woman has been transforming lives for decades by providing wheelchair related services to families across South Africa.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Shona McDonald has been changing lives since her own daughter, Shelly, was born with severe disabilities more than forty years ago. Her daughter was born with cerebral palsy because of medical negligence. At the time, doctors advised Shona to put her child in a home. She refused. She also did not take legal action against the hospital as she wanted to turn it into something positive. Instead, she approached the biomedical engineering department at UCT and asked them to help her build the first paediatric electric wheelchair in Africa.
metadata.Summary: She embarked on finding therapists and accessing information from abroad (it was before the internet) to try and understand what was possible and what was being done overseas. She researched how she could assist her daughter to sit up straight so she could see her mother, and she looked into ways her daughter could communicate more effectively. With the help of UCT, her child’s wheelchair for outdoors with full body support, that could go up and down, and in which she could move around herself, was built. Shelly was able to drive herself around by the age of eighteen months. Shona started an organization called Interface, that focused on helping non-verbal people communicate. She built different types of chairs for different children from her garage and did fundraising for those who couldn’t afford it. She realized the need was much greater than she had imagined. By 1992, she had outgrown her garage and realized she needed to turn it into a business. That was when she launched "Shonaquip Social Enterprise" which provides wheelchair related services to families across South Africa. Now, she has 85 people in her team and they work across seven countries. They make equipment for people living in rural areas, where wheelchairs are used off road. Furthermore, Shona's wheelchairs are designed to help children improve their function. Assistive devices are just a tool, but Shona’s work also looks at early child development, play for all, assistive technology and a parent network. She launched a parent network during Covid. She wanted to give parents knowledge and trains parents online three times a month. Nine hundred parents are trained every two weeks. They are upskilled and can run advocacy and anti bias workshops in their communities. Results of the training provide Shona with data that she reports to government to show where systems are failing. Shona has a fully inclusive team, with disabled people working in the factory as well. Her factory is in Ottery. She lives in Noordhoek with her three daughters. They all live on one property.
metadata.Further information: One man on the assembly team is an ex paralympic ping pong player. He had polio as a child so is paralysed from the waist down. Her whole focus is around how to ensure society values disabled people equally. There is also a lot of focus on making sure government has the right policies in place. When she started there was no such thing as a paediatric wheelchair tender. Now there is. Most children attending government hospitals, are now able to get one within a year. But, there are budget constraints. Shona has a wheelchair fund that helps kids who fall through the cracks. We will also speak to Vic McKinney who works with Shona. He was rendered quadriplegic after a devastating car accident in 1987. His father died in the accident. He became friends with Shona when she helped him design his first wheelchair. Together they confront stigma and are trying to change the lives of people with disabilities and bring an end to prejudice.
